overview.title: Welcome to Go for Meta Quest 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go for Meta Quest 👋 Go for Meta Quest runs Go programs on the Meta Quest 3 : a picture in each eye, a 3D scene that stays put in your room as you walk round it, and the controllers in your hands. It is the headset's side of the family: the program's loop, the controllers, and the tools that turn a Go program into a package the headset installs. Go Renderer draws, and talks to the headset through OpenXR, the open standard most headsets speak. Programs are built with the ordinary Go compiler and Android's NDK: no game engine, no Java. 🚧 A first step. The programs build, and their tests pass on a computer, but nothing has run on a headset yet. What was checked says exactly what. Is it for me? ✅ You have a Meta Quest 3 (or 3S) and want to put your own program in it. ✅ You want to see how a headset draws: two eyes, a pose for the head, a frame every 14 ms. ❌ You want to publish on the headset's store: this is for your own programs, installed with a cable. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time are new and want a program in the headset 🥽 The quest : a cube in your room, then an island to walk, in 5 levels 1 hour want to know what each piece does and what you need What is where 10 min All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest : five levels, from developer mode to walking an island What is where : the packages, the tools, what you need, what was checked, and what is not done yet 🚧 Not done yet See what is where . Words you will meet Word What it means Go A programming language. To try these projects you install it once, from go.dev, and type go run … in a terminal. Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Package ( .apk ) An Android application in one file. The headset runs Android underneath, so its programs are packages too. adb Android's tool to talk to a device over a cable: install a package, start it, read its log. OpenXR The open standard for headsets: it tells a program where the head and the hands are and takes a picture for each eye. Pose Where something is and which way it faces: a position in metres and a rotation. Quest The tutorial of these docs (not the headset!): short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go for Meta Quest is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS Go for Meta Quest (this one) Go on the Meta Quest 3 ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

the-quest.title: The headset quest
the-quest.text: The headset quest Put a Go program in a Meta Quest 3, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of Go for Meta Quest and ends with a package ( .apk ) you install on the headset. The quest map: a road from START through 5 levels — Developer, Two-eyed, Sculptor, Juggler and Explorer — to a final challenge, Headset owner We start by letting the computer talk to the headset, then paint each eye a colour of its own, put a cube in the room that stays where it is however you move, give each hand a cube of its own, walk an island with the sticks (and grow into a giant over it), and finally make a program of your own and share it. 🚧 Nothing here has run on a headset yet. Every level builds into a package, but the checkpoints describe what the program is written to do, not what was seen. If a checkpoint does not come true, what is where says what was and was not checked, and the log (level 1) says why. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the code , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus . Before you start You need: Why Where Go 1.25 or later The compiler; it builds for Android itself go.dev The Android SDK : build tools and a platform aapt2 , zipalign and apksigner make the package; the platform's android.jar is what its manifest is checked against Android Studio's SDK manager, or sdkmanager "build-tools;36.0.0" "platforms;android-37" The Android NDK Its clang compiles the C parts of Go Renderer's android and openxr sdkmanager "ndk;29.0.14206865" (any recent one) adb Installs and starts the package, and reads its log sdkmanager platform-tools A Meta Quest 3 (or 3S) and a USB-C cable Where it runs tools/build-apk.sh finds the SDK in ANDROID_HOME and the NDK in ANDROID_NDK_HOME (or in Homebrew's android-commandlinetools , on a Mac). Clone Go for Meta Quest; Go fetches Go Renderer by itself, at the commit go.mod names (its headset pieces are on its feature/openxr branch until it releases them): git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-meta-quest cd go-meta-quest Every program file starts with //go:build android : these programs only build for the headset. Level 1 · The Developer Mission Pieces Time The headset in developer mode, seen by the computer, and the OpenXR loader downloaded adb devices , tools/fetch-loader.sh 15 min The idea A headset is a locked room : it runs what its store sells. Developer mode is the key the maker gives programmers: with it, the headset accepts packages from a computer over the cable. The program will not talk to the headset's tracking directly. It talks to OpenXR , a standard many headsets share, through a small library from Khronos (the group behind OpenGL), the loader : it finds the headset's own OpenXR (its runtime ) and passes everything on. The loader goes inside every package. Do it Make yourself a developer in Meta's developer site (an organisation of your own is enough). In the Meta Horizon app on your phone: the headset › Headset settings › Developer mode , on. Connect the headset with the cable, put it on, and allow USB debugging for this computer. On the computer: adb devices # the headset, as "device" (not "unauthorized") tools/fetch-loader.sh # the newest OpenXR loader from Maven Central fetch-loader.sh reads which version is newest, downloads Khronos's openxr_loader_for_android , and keeps its arm64 library in third_party/openxr-loader/ (not committed: each clone fetches its own). Checkpoint adb devices lists the headset as device , and third_party/openxr-loader/arm64-v8a/libopenxr_loader.so exists. Bonus (optional): the headset's log Achievement unlocked: Developer Level 2 · The Two-eyed Mission Pieces Time Each eye a colour of its own, changing slowly app.Run , frame.Eyes , gles.Functions 5 min The idea A headset is two screens , one in front of each eye, and the program draws a picture for each, 72 times a second. The runtime hands the program, every frame, a framebuffer for each eye : the picture it will show there. Here each picture is only cleared to a colour, the simplest drawing there is, so that if it works, everything under it works: the package, the loader, the session, the pictures. The colours go round the colour wheel, the right eye half a turn behind the left: red in one eye, cyan in the other. Build it The program is cmd/clear in this repository: //go:build android package main import ( "log" "github.com/akrck02/go-meta-quest/app" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/gles" ) func main() { seconds := 0.0 err := app.Run(app.Options{ApplicationName: "Clear"}, func(frame app.Frame) bool { seconds += frame.Seconds // the time since the last frame if !frame.ShouldRender { // the runtime will not show this frame: draw nothing return true } for index, eye := range frame.Eyes { red, green, blue := eyeColour(index, seconds) // in cmd/clear/colours.go functions := frame.Functions functions.BindFramebuffer(gles.FramebufferTarget, eye.Target) functions.SetViewport(0, 0, eye.Width, eye.Height) functions.SetClearColor(red, green, blue, 1) functions.Clear(gles.ColorBufferBit | gles.DepthBufferBit) } return true // false would end the program }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } tools/build-apk.sh ./cmd/clear # build/clear.apk tools/install.sh build/clear.apk # installs, starts it, and shows its log Checkpoint Put the headset on: each eye sees a plain colour, a different one, both slowly changing. Close one eye, then the other. The headset's button with its logo brings the system's menu; choosing to leave ends the program. Bonus (optional): the same colour in both eyes Achievement unlocked: Two-eyed Level 3 · The Sculptor Mission Pieces Time A lit cube, standing still in the room as you move round it scene.Scene , camera.Rig , gles.SceneRenderer.DrawViews 10 min The idea On a screen, the camera is where the program says. In a headset, the camera is your head : the runtime says, every frame, where each eye is and which way it looks, in metres, in the room. The program draws the scene from there, so a cube put 1.5 m ahead of you stays 1.5 m from where it was, whatever you do: lean in, walk round it, look away and back. The room's floor is where the headset says it is, so the cube can stand at eye height. A rig ( camera.Rig ) is where the room is in the scene: here the scene is the room, one unit a metre. Each eye looks through a slightly lopsided window (it sees further to its own side than towards the nose), so each has its own projection. Go Renderer plans the frame once for both (which meshes are seen) and draws it twice. Build it The program is cmd/cube ; here is its heart (the cube's mesh and placing it are in cmd/cube/world.go ): made := newWorld() // a scene with a 30 cm cube, hidden until placed rig := camera.Rig{} // the room is the scene: one metre a unit var renderer *gles.SceneRenderer views := make([]gles.View, 2) poses := make([]graphics.Pose, 2) fields := make([]graphics.FieldOfView, 2) err := app.Run(app.Options{ApplicationName: "Cube"}, func(frame app.Frame) bool { if !frame.ShouldRender { return true } made.place(rig, frame.Head, frame.HeadTracked) // once the head is tracked: 1.5 m ahead, at its height if renderer == nil { created, err := gles.NewSceneRenderer(frame.Functions, overlay.Fonts{}) if err != nil { log.Print(err) return false } renderer = created } // The eyes' pictures turn colour to sRGB themselves: the renderer writes linear colour. renderer.LinearOutput = frame.SRGB for index, eye := range frame.Eyes { poses[index], fields[index] = eye.Pose, eye.Field views[index] = gles.View{Target: eye.Target, Width: eye.Width, Height: eye.Height, View: rig.EyeView(eye.Pose), Projection: graphics.PerspectiveFromFieldOfView(eye.Field, near, far), Eye: rig.EyePosition(eye.Pose)} } covering, aspect := camera.CoveringLens(rig, poses, fields, near, far) // one plan for both eyes renderer.DrawViews(made.scene, covering, aspect, views) return true }) tools/build-apk.sh ./cmd/cube tools/install.sh build/cube.apk Checkpoint An orange cube, the size of a box you could hold in both arms, an arm and a half ahead of you at eye height, turned so you see three faces, each shaded differently. Walk round it: it stays where it is, and you see its back. Its colours look like the colour, not washed out (that would be the colour turned to sRGB twice). Bonus (optional): bring the cube back Achievement unlocked: Sculptor Level 4 · The Juggler Mission Pieces Time A small cube in each hand frame.Hands , Grip , Tracked , rig.Place 5 min The idea The controllers are tracked like the head: each has a pose , where it is held ( Grip ) and where it points ( Aim ). A thing the program puts at a hand's grip pose moves with the hand. A controller the headset cannot see (behind your back, put down, asleep) is not tracked , and its cube hides. Build it It is already in cmd/cube : at the top of each frame, made.follow(rig, [2]graphics.Pose{frame.Hands[app.LeftHand].Grip, frame.Hands[app.RightHand].Grip}, [2]bool{frame.Hands[app.LeftHand].Tracked, frame.Hands[app.RightHand].Tracked}) and follow (in world.go ) puts each 5 cm cube at its hand with rig.Place(grip) , or hides it. Checkpoint A blue cube in your left hand and a green one in your right, inside the controllers' grips. Put a controller behind your back: its cube goes. Open the system's menu: the cubes stay drawn, but the program does not have the controllers until you come back ( frame.Focused is false). Bonus (optional): squeeze to grow Achievement unlocked: Juggler Level 5 · The Explorer Mission Pieces Time Stand on an island, walk it with the sticks, and grow into a giant over it sample.Island() , camera.RigWalk , rig.Scale , world.GroundHeight 15 min The idea Your room is small; the island is not. You can walk a few steps in the room, and the headset moves your eyes on the island just as far. To go further, the program moves the room itself on the island: that is the rig again (level 3). The left stick slides the room the way you look, so you glide over the ground; the right stick turns the room in steps around you. Never smoothly: a view that turns while your head does not makes many people queasy, a quick step does not. The program never moves your head . The headset says where it is, and the picture must follow it exactly, or the world swims. Two more things make it feel like a place. The room's floor follows the ground under your head , so you climb a hill as you walk up it ( world.GroundHeight ). And the rig's scale says how many of the island's units a metre of your room is: at 1 you are a person among the houses; at 20 you are a giant, the island is a model the size of a room, and your hands' cubes are twenty times bigger too. Switching keeps your head over the same spot of the ground, so you grow where you stand. Build it The program is cmd/explorer . Its world ( explorer.go ) is Go Renderer's sample island, the rig, a camera.RigWalk on the island's ground, and the two hand cubes of level 4: func newExplorer(world *scene.Scene) *explorer { made := &explorer{world: world, rig: startRig(world), // on the ground, south of the square views: make([]gles.View, 2), poses: make([]graphics.Pose, 2), fields: make([]graphics.FieldOfView, 2)} made.walk = camera.RigWalk{Ground: world.GroundHeight} // the floor follows the ground // … a cube for each hand, as in cmd/cube return made } // steer: Y or B switches between a person and a giant; the sticks walk and turn. func (made *explorer) steer(state *input.State, seconds float64, head graphics.Pose, headTracked bool) { if headTracked && (state.PadPressed(input.PadY) || state.PadPressed(input.PadB)) { made.rig = rescale(made.rig, head, otherScale(made.rig.Scale), made.walk.Ground) } made.walk.Update(state, seconds, head, &made.rig) } startRig and rescale are in places.go , plain Go with tests: the first finds the village square among the island's nodes and puts the room's floor on the ground twelve metres south of it, facing it; the second changes the scale and moves the room so the head stays over the same point. Every frame, main.go steers, follows the hands and draws both eyes as in level 3. The views are made into the same slices each frame, so a frame makes no new garbage for the collector to stop for; at 72 frames a second, a pause shows. The near plane grows with the scale: a giant's hands are twenty times further away in the island's units. tools/build-apk.sh ./cmd/explorer tools/install.sh build/explorer.apk Checkpoint You stand a short walk south of a paved square, in an afternoon light: the square ahead, the houses behind it, trees and the hill around, the sea and its fog far off. Push the left stick: you glide the way you look, up and down the slopes. Flick the right stick: the island turns a step around you. Walk in the room: you walk on the island. Press Y (or B ): you are a giant, the island at your feet, still over the same spot; press it again to be yourself. Bonus (optional): a faster giant Achievement unlocked: Explorer Final challenge · Headset owner A program of your own, in a module of your own, in the headset, and shared with the notices it must carry. Hint: tools/build-apk.sh builds from the folder it is run in, so it works for any module. Your module needs Go for Meta Quest, which brings Go Renderer with it. Rare achievement unlocked: Headset owner Well done All six achievements: Developer, Two-eyed, Sculptor, Juggler, Explorer and Headset owner You built Go for a headset: a picture in each eye, a cube that stays in the room, the controllers in your hands, and an island to walk, as a person or as a giant. Ideas to keep going Idea Difficulty Hint A cube that spins ⭐ Turn made.cube.Transform a little every frame by frame.Seconds , and set the node's Moving The island at night ⭐ sample.Night() instead of sample.Island() A scale in between ⭐⭐ A third size on X, say 5: the island the size of a house Jump to a place ⭐⭐ On A, move rig.Position so the head stands over another node of the island ( nodePosition ), the floor on its ground Troubleshooting You see Why, and what to do adb devices lists the headset as unauthorized Put it on and allow USB debugging for this computer The program opens in a flat window The package lacks com.oculus.intent.category.VR , or it was built from another manifest: build it with tools/build-apk.sh It closes at once; the log says the loader is missing libopenxr_loader.so is not in the package: run tools/fetch-loader.sh and build again build constraints exclude all Go files , or the program prints that it runs on a Meta Quest These programs build for Android only: use tools/build-apk.sh , not go build Colours look washed out, too light The colour was turned to sRGB twice: set renderer.LinearOutput = frame.SRGB On the island, you stand inside the ground or float over it The floor follows the ground under the head, and the head stands as high above it as it is above the room's floor: check the room's floor in the headset's settings (a guardian drawn at the wrong height puts the floor there too) The cube is on the floor, or above you It is placed at the head's height on the first frame shown: start the program standing (or sitting) as you mean to look at it, or bring it back (level 3's bonus) ← All the documentation

what-is-where.title: What is where
what-is-where.text: What is where The packages of Go for Meta Quest, the programs and tools it comes with, what you need to build for the headset, and what was checked: so far, only on a computer. What is where Piece What it does app The program loop. Run starts Go Renderer's headset activity ( android.RunHeadset : no window, an OpenGL ES 3 context on its own thread), opens the OpenXR session there ( openxr.Open ), and goes round: it reads the session's news; while the session does not run (the headset off the head, starting, paused) it sleeps 10 ms; while it runs it begins a frame, reads the controllers (only while the program has them), calls the program's step, and ends the frame. It stops when the runtime asks the program to leave; when the step returns false or a frame fails it first asks the runtime to stop the session ( RequestExit ) and hands back empty frames until it has, two seconds at most. It closes the session on the drawing thread. Each Frame carries the input state (the controllers as a game pad), the head's pose and whether it is tracked, both hands, the seconds since the last frame (from the display times, at most a tenth of a second), whether the program has the controllers, whether the frame will be shown, the two eyes (pose, field of view, framebuffer), whether those encode sRGB, and OpenGL ES. Options.Panels asks for panels by their size in pixels ( PanelSize , at most openxr.MostPanels , checked before any is made); they are made when the session opens and every Frame.Panels holds them in that order, to place ( Pose , FitWidth , Shown ) and draw into ( Target , only when the picture changes). Frame.Vibrate(hand, amplitude, duration) shakes a controller. cmd/clear The first program: each eye cleared to a colour of its own going slowly round the colour wheel, the right eye half a turn behind. No renderer: it checks the package, the loader, the session and the pictures with nothing else in the way. cmd/cube A lit 30 cm cube 1.5 m ahead of where the player first looked, at the head's height, that stays there in the room; a 5 cm cube in each tracked controller's grip. Drawn by Go Renderer's gles.SceneRenderer.DrawViews : the frame planned once from a lens covering both eyes ( camera.CoveringLens ), then drawn in each eye with its own lopsided projection. cmd/room The cube of cmd/cube in the player's own room: it opens the session with Options.Passthrough , and while Frame.ShowsRoom it draws with gles.SceneRenderer.SeeThrough , so the headset's cameras show the room wherever the cube is not. The first step of mixed reality; on a headset without passthrough it is the cube on black. explore Walks a player through any scene.Scene at room scale: Run(world, Options) is the whole program loop. camera.RigWalk walks the rig with the left stick the way the head looks and turns it in steps around the head with the right one, the floor on the scene's walkable ground under the head ( world.GroundHeight ). Options.WalkMetresSecond walks faster, and Options.TurnRadiansSecond turns smoothly about the head instead of in steps (a program whose right stick scrolls a panel feeds it 0 sideways meanwhile). Y or B switches between a person (scale 1) and a giant ( GiantScale , 20 by default), the head kept over the same point of the ground. The near plane grows with the scale, Far is the scene's; a cube in each tracked hand, as in cmd/cube . Options.Start is where the room stands at the start: the program decides. A frame's steering makes no garbage (tested); the views are made in the same slices every frame. Show explores another scene (the hands go with the player); Move puts the room somewhere else in the same one, at any scale. A program with its own loop (panels, say) calls New , then Steer , Follow and Views every frame instead of Run . place Where things stand, as sums on poses, tested anywhere. In the scene: RigWithHeadAt puts the head over a point of the floor looking a way, at a scale; TurnedAround and RescaledAround turn or resize the person about their head, which stays over the same point; RoomPoint is a point of the scene in the room and Keeping moves the rig so one is at a point of the room; TurnedAbout and ResizedAbout turn or resize a model about its middle; ModelAhead puts a scene on a table ahead of the head; StandingBefore sets the person down before a point, on their side, facing it. In the room: Ahead (a panel called up), FacingHead (a label), LeaningBack and UnderEyes (a strip low ahead, leaned back toward the eyes), Following (a yaw that follows the head only once it looks well away), PalmFacing and OverPalm (a menu over a hand whose palm is turned to the face), HeightForAngle ; and HeadYaw , YawFacing , AngleBetween , AnglesOf . mirror A finger on a picture of the headset's screen points as the right controller does. Listen reads lines from a Unix socket ( @name is Android's abstract namespace, reached with adb forward ): down , move and up with a point of the left eye's picture, look with two (two fingers dragged), mark with one or off . Touches hands them to the frames one change at a time (a quick tap still presses and lets go), Hand is the controller the finger is, Carry carries out a drag (a panel it began on swings about the eye; elsewhere it says how far to turn the person), MarkPose places the mark, and Direction and PicturePoint go between the eye's picture and the room. selftest Goes through a program as a person would, with controllers of its own. A Runner runs Step s (ready, act, check), each settling a while before its check: PointAt points the right hand from beside the head at a point of the room and pulls the trigger once, Press presses a button for a frame, PressMenu the menu, HoldPalmUp turns the left palm to the face. A program calls Drive before its frame and Check after; in the headset it reads the runner's Pad instead of the real controllers. AskedFor tells whether a file was put in the program's folder with adb, to run it there. cmd/explorer Go Renderer's sample island ( sample.Island() , its afternoon light and fog) explored with explore . The player starts on the ground twelve metres south of the village square, facing it, at a person's size. pointer Points at panels with a controller, as a laser. FromAim is the ray along a hand's aim (-Z); HitPanel finds the pixel it meets on a panel, from the side it faces, and how far. A Pointer feeds an interface's own input.State from one hand each frame: the cursor to that pixel, the trigger as the left button (pressed past 0.7, let go under 0.3), the stick up and down as the wheel ( ScrollNotchesPerSecond at full tilt); when the ray leaves the panel a held button is let go and the cursor leaves the interface. The state's window is the panel's picture. PointAtNearest points one hand at several Interface s (a panel, its input and its pointer) at once: the nearest shown one the ray meets has it, the others let go. SceneRay is the hand's ray in the scene, through the rig; AimAt aims a hand of a program's own at a point; PanelPoint is a pixel of a panel in the room. A Beam is a thin unlit bar from the hand to what it meets, placed through the rig, hidden on an untracked hand. Pointing makes no garbage (tested). cmd/panel A board of six tiles floating 1.5 m ahead over the sample island, a panel drawn by gles.FlatRenderer (linear colour): the right controller's beam points at it, the tile under it is outlined with a light buzz, the trigger lights a tile or puts it out with a stronger one. The board is drawn again only when it changes; the sticks walk the island while it stays with you. tools/AndroidManifest.xml The manifest every package gets: Android's NativeActivity loading libmain.so , the com.oculus.intent.category.VR category (immersive, not a flat window), head tracking required, com.oculus.supportedDevices (Quest 3 and 3S), com.oculus.vr.focusaware on the activity (the program keeps running, shown, while the system's menu is up), landscape, kept out of the recent list, never recreated by a configuration change (the session holds the activity), one at a time, no Java. It names the OpenXR permissions and the broker's providers the loader asks which runtime to load. tools/fetch-loader.sh Reads Maven Central's newest org.khronos.openxr:openxr_loader_for_android , downloads it, and keeps its arm64 libopenxr_loader.so and its licence in third_party/openxr-loader/ (not committed). A version can be named: tools/fetch-loader.sh 1.1.65 . tools/build-apk.sh Builds a program into build/<name>.apk , from the folder it runs in: go build -buildmode=c-shared with the NDK's clang and 16 KB pages, the manifest linked by aapt2 against the newest platform's android.jar , the program's library and the loader stored uncompressed under lib/arm64-v8a/ , aligned to 16 KB ( zipalign -P 16 ), signed with the debug key (made if missing). Its id is io.github.akrck02.metaquest.<name> and its label the folder's name, unless APK_ID and APK_LABEL say otherwise: a program in a module of its own builds with the same script, under its own id. tools/install.sh Installs a package on the headset with adb install -r , starts it (by APK_ID when it was built with one), and shows the log under the tags Go and OpenXR . What is not here is Go Renderer's, as on the 3DS: the drawing ( gles ), the activity ( android ), the OpenXR session, its swapchains and the controllers ( openxr ), the poses and the eyes' projections ( graphics ), the rig and the covering lens ( camera ). What you need Go 1.25 or later. The Android SDK's build tools ( aapt2 , zipalign with -P , so 35 or later; apksigner ) and a platform, in ANDROID_HOME ; the NDK in ANDROID_NDK_HOME . On a Mac, Homebrew's android-commandlinetools is found without them. Go Renderer's headset pieces, which go.mod fetches by itself: a commit of its feature/openxr branch, until they are released. adb , and a Meta Quest 3 or 3S in developer mode. tools/build-apk.sh ./cmd/cube tools/install.sh build/cube.apk What was checked On a Meta Quest 3 (Android 14, API 34, connected with adb in developer mode), from the system's own log and the headset's screen captures ( adb exec-out screencap -p , both eyes side by side): Both packages start immersive. The loader finds the runtime, and the session goes IDLE → READY → SYNCHRONIZED → VISIBLE → FOCUSED within a tenth of a second. cmd/clear : each eye shows its own colour, the right eye half a turn behind on the colour wheel. With the system's menu open the session drops to VISIBLE and the program keeps drawing under it; going home stops the session (STOPPING → IDLE) and the program waits without spinning. cmd/cube : the cube and both hands' cubes are drawn in each eye, over the horizon's colour, with near things (the hands) further apart between the eyes than far ones, as they should be. Frames keep the headset's pace: 72 a second, none stale, the program's processor time under 1 ms a frame (the runtime's own VrApi line in adb logcat ). cmd/room : not checked on a headset. It builds for Android (its library compiles with the passthrough's C); whether the room shows behind the cube needs the headset. cmd/explorer : the island is drawn in each eye at 72 frames a second, the program's processor time under 1 ms a frame, seen through the headset's screen recording ( adb exec-out screenrecord ) with the headset lying on a desk, so without the sticks. cmd/panel : the board is shown over the island, its own colours (not washed out) and its title readable, at 72 frames a second, with the haptics server connected and no error in the log. The headset lay on a desk: pointing, clicking and the buzzes are not tried with hands yet. With the headset on, the cube was seen working as it should. Leaving from the system's menu (Quit) is not tried yet. On a Mac (Go 1.27, NDK 29, build tools 37, platform android-37, OpenXR loader 1.1.65): go vet ./... and go test ./... pass: the loop's decisions (leave, wait, frame), the clock (the first frame, 72 frames a second, a long pause, time going back, a restart), the eyes' colours, the cube's world (its size, faces pointing out, placed ahead at eye height and staying there, the hands' cubes following tracked hands only), the island's start (on the ground south of the square), and the exploration's (the options' defaults, the giant and back with the head over the same point, Y waiting for a tracked head, a second of the stick walking 1.5 m on the ground, the views and their covering lens, no allocations while steering). go vet for Android (arm64, with the NDK's clang) passes on every package. tools/fetch-loader.sh downloads the loader; tools/build-apk.sh builds build/clear.apk , build/cube.apk and build/explorer.apk . Each holds the manifest, libmain.so and libopenxr_loader.so stored uncompressed; zipalign -c -P 16 and apksigner verify accept them, and both libraries' segments are aligned to 16 KB. On an Android 16 phone emulator (arm64), both packages install and start: the Go runtime runs main , the drawing thread gets its OpenGL ES 3 context, and the OpenXR loader starts and asks the runtime broker for a runtime. A phone has none, so the program ends there, cleanly, with openxr.instance-not-created in the log ( adb logcat -s Go ). The manifest's SDK levels (minimum 32, target 34) follow Meta's documentation as last read; the headset above runs API 34. Not yet Walking, turning and the giant tried with the headset on. Pointing at a panel, clicking and the buzzes, tried with the headset on; a Go UI interface on a panel (the pieces are there: pointer feeds an input.State as Go UI reads it). The headset's own settings: refresh rate, foveated rendering, passthrough. Drawing both eyes in one pass (multiview), sound, storage. A frame entirely without garbage: camera.CoveringLens (Go Renderer's) still makes two small slices a frame, and explore cannot avoid them. Programs on other headsets: the OpenXR part is standard, but the manifest is Meta's.
